title: A Gilded Age Holdout on West 57th Street
author: Lexi Zotomayor
excerpt: A chance walk past a lone Midtown brownstone turns into a quiet meditation on memory, disappearing architecture, and what New York loses when history gets in the way of real estate.
bodyText:
Walking through Manhattan puts me in a mild trance. My mind drifts backward and forward in time, marveling at the older buildings that still stand despite the steady pressure of New York real estate to tear them down.

On a recent afternoon, on my way to a doctor’s appointment near Columbus Circle, I passed a solitary brownstone wedged between skyscrapers on West 57th Street. A faded marquee out front showed that a restaurant had once taken up the ground floor, though the place looked long empty. Surrounded by scaffolding and the noise of nearby construction, the clay-colored building seemed to be making a quiet stand on its own. I figured it predated my generation—perhaps even the great department stores like Saks, Gimbels, and Bonwit Teller. Out of habit, I took a few snapshots with my phone,wanting to keep a record of a building holding out like a tiny Sparta.

Days passed, and everyday errands pushed the brownstone out of my head. Then, late one night, while scrolling through social media before sleep, I came across a post urging people to oppose the demolition of a historic house. I looked closely at the photograph. That stubborn brownstone had a name: No. 35 West 57th Street, built in 1891 as a wedding gift for Maria Louise Vanderbilt Shepard and William Jay Schieffelin. After standing for more than a century as one of the last Gilded Age mansions in Midtown, it was finally facing the wrecking ball.

I was not born in this country, yet the news brought a sharp sense of loss—a grief for an American heritage so easily leveled and forgotten. It is hard to explain why a person mourns bricks and mortar from another century, or why a passerby feels invested in keeping old walls upright when economics tells history it is time to go.

We cannot bring back time, and surely that counts for something. There is no price tag to put on these physical reminders of an earlier era, which speak not only to the skill of their architects, but to the ambition of the business figures who built the modern city. My objection, of course, is only a whisper. I am just an admirer of the arts and humanities, left once again to nurse a small heartbreak for a period long gone.

![Vanderbilt-Shepard-Shiefflin House at 35 West 57th Street, New York City ](/assets/uploads/cms/vanderbilt-shepard-shieffelin-house.png "This five-story Beaux Arts style mansion was a wedding gift  by Margaret Vanderbilt Shepard for her daughter, Maria Louisa and her husband William Jay Schieffelin. The couple lived at his address until 1899 when Samuel Bowne bought the property when the Shiefflin couple moved in the upper east side. ")
